subject: Sampling a multinormal truncated to lie inside a 2D polygon

messages.author: 1090ec6e2018fcc1
messages.subject: Sampling a multinormal truncated to lie inside a 2D polygon
parts:
I'm trying to write some Stan code to sample a 2D multinormal distribution truncated to lie inside a 2D polygon. If x is a 2D sample vector, the polygon vertices are the columns of the matrix V, and z is a simplex vector whose length equals the number of vertices, then the polygon constraint can be described by x = V*z. In other words, x is constrained to be an interpolation between the vertices. Here is my Stan code:

data {
  int nDim;
  int nVerts;
  real mu;
  real sigma;
  matrix[nDim,nVerts] V;
}
parameters {
  simplex[nVerts] z;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[nDim] x;
  x <- V*z;
}
model {
  // mu ~ normal(x, sigma);
  x ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

I provide two versions of the model equation, but both fail for any polygon beyond three vertices. When there are three vertices, there is a unique linear mapping between x and z, so Stan works well. But for more than three vertices, V has a null space, meaning that there are a multiplicity of z solutions corresponding to any x. Since z is a simplex, the volume of this null space is finite, and varies with the value of x. If I use the volume of this null space as the reciprocal of the Jacobian and enter this manually using increment_log_prob(), then the sampling is correct.

I'm wondering if there is a better way to sample this problem that avoids the expensive manual Jacobian calculation. Any suggestions?

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling a multinormal truncated to lie inside a 2D polygon
parts:
Hi Michael,

I see that you did not get a reply (at least on list) so I will write up
my experience with something similar. Recently I was working on a
problem where the parameters in a 2D space were constrained in a
(somewhat) irregular hexagon with two parallel slides which I could put
together from 2 trapezoids, which I then mapped to a rectangle. It was a
bit of algebra, and the Jacobian was not continuous where the two
trapezoids met, but otherwise it was tractable; however, it was also
clear that generalizing it would be extremely tedious.

However, during the holiday break I managed rewrite my parameters in a
way that (1) is easier to handle, (2) makes more sense in the given
context, (3) is easier to interpret and (4) samples faster (higher n_eff
for same number of draws). I don't know your problem domain, but now
instead of thinking of extremely clever transformations my first
approach is to rewrite the problem.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 1090ec6e2018fcc1
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling a multinormal truncated to lie inside a 2D polygon
parts:
Tamas,

Thank you for your insight. My real quest is to find a general method for sampling a distribution subject to truncation on a general N-dimensional polytope. My recent focus is to implement this efficiently in Stan. While I've found some clever transformations that are efficient for particular sub problems, the only general approach I've found is too slow for most applications. In lieu of a Stan implementation, I have a general implementation based on Gibbs' sampling that is reasonably fast for polytopes with a small number of vertices, but becomes too slow as the number of vertices increases. I only posted to this list in the hope that maybe there is a clever general formulation for computing the Jacobian for linear change of variables where there is a null space in the new coordinates.

Michael

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling a multinormal truncated to lie inside a 2D polygon
parts:
This discussion's great!

As Michael says, in general you need the Jacobian of the z |-> x
transform because you are placing the density on the transformed x.

As Tamas says, if you can find a clever reparameterization, you're
better off doing that.

Maybe Michael Betancourt can answer the general question about
the Jacobians.

One thing we could conceivably do in the future is allow
user-defined transforms where we compute the Jacobian
automatically --- it won't be super-efficient compared to
doing it by hand, because we'll have to compute a Jacobian
using higher-order autodiff (not too bad --- N with a relatively
high constant) and then take its log determinant (not so
good --- N^3 with the same high constant). And we'd probably have
to require the user to write the function as a pure vector function
with data parameters:

vector my_transform(vector theta, vector x, int[] x_int);

where theta is the vector of parameters to transform and
x and x_int are data. Ideally we should allow this data stuff to
be optional everywhere. I just updated our longer-term to-do list
to include this item:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Longer-Term-To-Do-List

- Bob

messages.author: 1090ec6e2018fcc1
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling a multinormal truncated to lie inside a 2D polygon
parts:
Tamas,

Here is the basic idea. Let's say you want to sample x from a multinormal, but want to constrain the samples to lie in a polytope whose vertices, v_i, are the columns of a matrix V. Then the allowed region for x is defined by x = V*nu, where the vector nu is a simplex. Then the naive Stan code for this problem is

parameters {
  simplex[n_vertices] nu;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[n_dim] x;
  x <- V*nu;
}
model {
  x ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

The Stan compiler will inform you that the Jacobian for the transformation from x to nu must be input manually, but for interesting cases the dimension of nu is much larger than the dimension of x, so standard methods can't be used for computing this Jacobian. Since the transformation is linear, the actual values of the derivatives are irrelevant. What is important is the number of nu values that satisfy x=V*nu for a given value of x. I term this multiplicity of nu values the volume of the nu null space for any given x. The Jacobian is then J=1/vol(x). I coded this formula and get the correct sampling (modulo some divide-by-zero issues near the polytope boundary). The main problem is that the computation of this volume is very slow.

So while my formulation is correct, I'm wondering if there is a faster way to implement a solution for the general case. I recognize that there are good solutions for particular polytopes, but I am seeking a global formulation. I've seen reflection boundary conditions being used in the literature for Hamiltonian formulations of problems of this sort, but I'm not sure if that is the best approach for Stan either.

Michael

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling a multinormal truncated to lie inside a 2D polygon
parts:
If n_vertices >> n_dim then you'll have a hugely non-identified posterior which will
be hard to sample unless the Jacobians are sufficient to identify the problem.  As
Tamas notes some analytic work will go a long way -- if nu is a simplex then V * nu 
usually spans a lower dimensional simplex (depending on the null space of V, there
are some weird edge cases).  If you can parameterize that lower-dimensional simplex
directly then sampling will fly.
On Jan 11, 2016, at 8:12 PM, Michael Prange <pra...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

Tamas,

Here is the basic idea. Let's say you want to sample x from a multinormal, but want to constrain the samples to lie in a polytope whose vertices, v_i, are the columns of a matrix V. Then the allowed region for x is defined by x = V*nu, where the vector nu is a simplex. Then the naive Stan code for this problem is

parameters {
  simplex[n_vertices] nu;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[n_dim] x;
  x <- V*nu;
}
model {
  x ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

The Stan compiler will inform you that the Jacobian for the transformation from x to nu must be input manually, but for interesting cases the dimension of nu is much larger than the dimension of x, so standard methods can't be used for computing this Jacobian. Since the transformation is linear, the actual values of the derivatives are irrelevant. What is important is the number of nu values that satisfy x=V*nu for a given value of x. I term this multiplicity of nu values the volume of the nu null space for any given x. The Jacobian is then J=1/vol(x). I coded this formula and get the correct sampling (modulo some divide-by-zero issues near the polytope boundary). The main problem is that the computation of this volume is very slow.

So while my formulation is correct, I'm wondering if there is a faster way to implement a solution for the general case. I recognize that there are good solutions for particular polytopes, but I am seeking a global formulation. I've seen reflection boundary conditions being used in the literature for Hamiltonian formulations of problems of this sort, but I'm not sure if that is the best approach for Stan either.

Michael

On Mon, Jan 11, 2016 at 2:08 PM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:

Can you tell us about the underlying problem and give a bit more
context? First, I am frankly curious, second, you may get advice on how

that's what you need to estimate, but in some fields there is sometimes
a possibility of using another model that is not inferior to the

Best,

Tamas
